title: The wild creation (Psalm 104)
hookLine: wine to gladden hearts, rocks for the badgers, a sea full of creatures

cards: Lions roaring in the dark, asking for their dinner. Wild goats on cliffs too steep for anyone else. A stork nesting at the top of a fir tree.
Donkeys drinking at a stream, birds singing in the branches above them. Then sunrise: the lions slink home to their dens, and a man heads out to work until evening.
Out at sea, ships sail past an enormous creature that's simply playing in the waves. It sounds like the script for a nature documentary.
It's a psalm, an ancient song of Israel, looking at the natural world for its own sake.

teach.b: Psalm one hundred four walks through creation roughly in the order of Genesis one: light, sky, waters, earth, plants, creatures, sun and moon. But where Genesis is spare, this psalm is crowded and noisy.
Listen to verse eighteen in the King James Bible: "The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies." Conies.
The Hebrew is shaphan, usually identified as the rock hyrax: a small, furry, round animal that lives among rocks. Some translations call it a badger. Whatever you call it, God made the rocks for it.
Not for us. That's the striking thing about this psalm. Humans show up as one creature among many.
People get wine "that maketh glad the heart of man," and oil, and bread. Fine. But the lions get their meat from God too, and the storks get the fir trees.
Then the sea: "There go the ships: there is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein." Leviathan, the sea monster that frightens readers elsewhere in the Bible, made here to play.

teach.h: IN WISDOM HAST THOU MADE THEM ALL
teach.b: And the center of the psalm: "O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all."

teach.h: O LORD, HOW MANIFOLD ARE THY WORKS!
teach.b: Some scholars hear echoes of an older Egyptian hymn to the sun in this psalm; if so, the psalmist took that wonder and turned it toward the one God.
Orthodox Christians open their evening service, Vespers, with this psalm, and churches read it at Pentecost, for verse thirty: thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created.

how: Orthodox Christians chant Psalm 104 at the opening of Vespers each evening, and many churches pray it at Pentecost and in services of thanksgiving for creation.

games.q: who lives where in the psalm — tap the pairs.

s: the Hebrew shaphan is usually identified as the rock hyrax, a small rock-dwelling animal.
Psalm 104 says leviathan was made to play in the sea
"there is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein."
in this psalm, everything in nature exists for humans
the rocks are for the conies, the hills for the goats, and the lions get their meat from God.

games.q: you're writing a song about creation. you've reached the sea, and the well-known sea monster, leviathan. what do you say about it?
o: God made it to play in the sea.
games.why: Psalm 104:26: "there is that leviathan, whom thou hast made to play therein." the monster becomes a creature at play.

practice: Look out a window, step outside, or call to mind one creature from the last few days, a pigeon, a spider in the corner, an ant on the counter, and watch it, or picture it.
How does it move, what is it looking for, where will it sleep tonight? Don't call it useful or a nuisance; if you pray, say in wisdom hast thou made them all, and if you don't, simply watch.

wordCard.voice: Leviathan. The sea monster that Psalm one hundred four pictures made by God simply to play in the waves, among lions, goats, conies and storks, all fed by him.

orig.note: Hebrew: the rock hyrax, the King James Bible's coney. the psalm says God made the rocks its refuge.

carryVoice: Your line: all made in wisdom. Even the ones you'd shoo away. Four hundred thirty-two days, done.
